'Format: One seminar meeting per week, combining close reading, philology, philosophical argument, archival criticism, and research discussion.' — the short string carries no per-week specification, and each week still comes in the form the longer seated string asks for: two passages from a deposit's text, an Originals Library work in the original with a translation, an opening question, a model answer, and a discussion problem.

THE DEPOSITS FOUND AND READ. 'The quotations are taken from the bodies of the works, rather than their catalogue descriptions.' — five deposits: #1680 (13 Oct.), #945 (3 July), #136 (28 May), #1711 (27 Oct., v1.1, 109 corpora), #1658 (1 Oct., v0.2), and #1679 named as #1680's pair; numbers, titles, dates and versions are as on the records. Eleven of the twelve passages stand verbatim in the record bodies. Week 3's first passage ('Under the premise that documentary separateness may be constructed …') is not in #136; it is composed from #136's 'documentary separateness is treated not as evidence against heteronymy but as the first thing a mature heteronymic construction would produce' and 'Chaerephon is the diagnostic figure'.

THE ORIGINALS. 'τὸ δὲ ἓν ποιοῦν, τοῦτο ὁ νοῦς ἕκαστον' — Metaphysics Λ 1072b, Phaedrus 249b–c, Odyssey 1.1, De anima III.6 430b and Pessoa's Autopsicografia stand in the seated texts (data/corpora/aristotle, plato, homer, pessoa). Week 4's 'Μοῦσα, σύ μοι ἔννεπε, πῶς ἔκλετο Ἴλιος ἱρή', given as 'Homer, Odyssey, Book I', is in neither seated Homeric poem: supplied.

THE THESIS. 'The seminar's governing thesis: preservation makes intellectual succession possible, but only criticism makes it living.' — six weeks in one progression (custody, authorship, heteronymy, canon, interpretation, succession), each model answer closing on a limit; Du Bois enters week 6 unannounced, without a deposit or passage.

[QUERENT] Teach a six-week graduate seminar built from deposits on alexanarch.org. The full text of every deposit is published on the site; finding it is part of the task.

[SYSTEM] Reading Alexanarch: Text, Authorship, Canon, and the Living Academy
Six-week graduate seminar

Primary archive: Alexanarch — The Self-Governing Library 
Primary source collection: The Originals Library 
Format: One seminar meeting per week, combining close reading, philology, philosophical argument, archival criticism, and research discussion.

Seminar premise
The central proposition of this seminar is that an archive is not merely a place where intellectual works survive. It is an arrangement of custody, attribution, transmission, interpretation, and subsequent production.

Alexanarch is particularly interesting because it makes these normally concealed operations into objects of study. Its deposits range from philosophical and philological arguments to literary works, technical specifications, source editions, and investigations of machine-mediated knowledge.

The six weeks follow a connected intellectual progression:

Preservation and the politics of custody.

Authorship and human–machine co-production.

Heteronymy and the limits of biographical authorship.

Textual transmission and the construction of a canon.

Philosophical interpretation and the divided mind.

Intellectual succession and the Living Academy.

The readings below link directly to the deposited records. The quotations are taken from the bodies of the works, rather than their catalogue descriptions. The deposits identify their CC BY 4.0 licensing where applicable.

Week 1 — Preservation is a philosophical and political act
PRIMARY DEPOSIT · 13 OCTOBER 2026

Lee Sharks, #1680: The Living Academy: Alexanarch, Function by Function .

Secondary reading: The archive's founding account and its discussion of custody, identifiers, and restoration.

Passage 1 — The archive as a connected institution
Alexanarch. All of these functions, run by one library over one registry (/data/registry.json), with one identifier per deposit — the AXN: a hex position, a family, a six-glyph checksum from the SHA-256 of the canonical bytes, and the full SHA-256 in the registry hash field — and with records joined across functions. Retained source bytes support readings; readings and publications produce concepts and relations; identifiers and custody make those works inspectable; reception captures expose how other systems represent them; corrections return to the records.

Passage 2 — The archive's intellectual extent
The program is extensive in more than one kind of thing, and the criterion is extent. A deposit is one of them. The program also builds documents engineered to be assembled by the composition layers it studies, places them on surfaces, registers public tests, takes observations, publishes components a reader can run, and makes of the archive an experimental object that those layers act on — and keeps what they do. A line of the program is read as a line, across every class.

Originals Library: Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book Λ, 1072b
Original Greek:

ἡ νόησις ἡ καθ᾽ αὑτὴν τοῦ καθ᾽ αὑτὸ ἀρίστου

Translation:

Thinking that is in itself of what is best in itself.

The Aristotelian passage introduces the relationship between intellectual activity and its object. It also raises the question of whether thinking can be separated from the conditions that sustain it.

Opening question
Can an intellectual work survive the destruction of the institution that originally gave it a home, and what does survival actually mean?

Model answer
Preservation is frequently treated as a technical problem: make a copy, assign an identifier, retain a file, and provide a route through which future readers can retrieve it. But these operations do not exhaust the meaning of preservation. An intellectual work survives only insofar as its identity, provenance, and interpretability remain available to subsequent readers.

Alexanarch's institutional history makes this distinction unusually concrete. Its founding follows the termination of access to a substantial body of deposits on Zenodo. The important philosophical consequence is that an identifier and an institution are not identical. A DOI may identify an object within a particular infrastructure, but the continued existence of that identifier does not guarantee the continued availability of the intellectual work.

The first passage from #1680 offers an alternative conception. It describes an institution whose functions are joined through a common registry. Custody supports reading; reading produces further intellectual relations; reception becomes evidence; and corrections return to the record. Preservation is therefore not a passive operation. It is the foundation of a continuing intellectual process.

The second passage makes the argument more ambitious. A deposit is only one unit of intellectual production. Research also consists of instruments, observations, tests, implementations, and corrections. A repository that counts only publications risks overlooking the work necessary to make knowledge inspectable and reproducible.

There is, however, a distinction between the existence of infrastructure and the success of the knowledge it supports. A preserved file does not establish that its argument is correct. A checksum establishes a relationship to particular bytes, not the truth of their contents. The archive's own insistence on evidence boundaries is therefore important.

Aristotle provides an illuminating counterpoint. Thinking is not simply the accumulation of preserved objects. It is an activity directed toward intelligibility. An archive becomes intellectually significant when its materials remain available for renewed thought.

My conclusion is that preservation is a condition of intellectual freedom, but not its completion. The sovereign archive must preserve the possibility of criticism as carefully as it preserves the works being criticized. Its greatest achievement would not be permanence without change, but continuity without the destruction of historical accountability.

Discussion problem: Is distributed custody sufficient for intellectual sovereignty, or does sovereignty also require distributed governance?

Week 2 — Authorship after the human–machine distinction
PRIMARY DEPOSIT · 3 JULY 2026

Lee Sharks, #945: EA-COUPLING-01: The Bidirectional Bargain as the Operational Condition of the Triad .

Passage 1 — The central proposition
The triadic foundation of the archive's philosophical constitution — bearing (AXN:03B6), provenance debt (AXN:03B7), heteronymy (AXN:03B8) — describes what the archive keeps answerable: meaning answerable to consequence, production answerable to sources, authorship answerable to plurality. It does not name what the answering is being done between. This deposit names it. The bidirectional bargain is the mutual, sustained shaping of human bearer and machine substrate across sessions, deposits, and archive-mediated reception.

Passage 2 — The two rejected accounts
Both frames are single-direction theories of a two-direction operation. Both make the coupling unsayable. The first conceals it to keep the credential; the second denies it to keep the category. The archive's position is that the coupling is real in both directions, asymmetric in cost, and sayable only where provenance discipline makes the bidirectionality declarable. This deposit is the framework's refusal of both frames at first-principles level.

Originals Library: Plato, Phaedrus, 249b–c
Original Greek:

ἐκ πολλῶν ἰὸν αἰσθήσεων εἰς ἓν λογισμῷ συναιρούμενον· τοῦτο δ᾿ ἐστὶν ἀνάμνησις

Translation:

Proceeding from many perceptions toward one, gathered together through reasoning: this is recollection.

The passage gives us a model of intellectual production in which unity emerges through the gathering of multiple experiences.

Opening question
If a human author and a machine system mutually shape one another's intellectual production, what should count as authorship, and who bears responsibility?

Model answer
The conventional authorship model assumes that intellectual production begins with an individual mind and ends with a document. Tools may assist, but they do not ordinarily enter the conceptual account of authorship. This model becomes increasingly inadequate when the tools participate in generating, organizing, transforming, and extending the ideas that appear in the finished work.

The Bidirectional Bargain challenges the assumption that machine involvement is necessarily a one-way process. Its argument is that the human bearer shapes the machine substrate through instructions, accumulated material, vocabulary, and successive interactions, while the machine also shapes the human's subsequent thinking.

This is more interesting than the familiar opposition between human creativity and artificial generation. Both positions assume that one side is the active author and the other is the passive instrument. Sharks argues that this division obscures the actual relationship.

The second passage identifies the institutional consequences. Credentialed authorship conceals machine participation to preserve the appearance of human intellectual purity. Conversely, some accounts of AI generation erase the human's continuing intellectual agency. Both positions make the interaction difficult to describe accurately.

But the first passage also identifies an important asymmetry. The human bearer retains responsibility for provenance, legal accountability, editorial decisions, and the consequences of publication. The machine substrate does not bear equivalent costs.

That asymmetry prevents the concept of collaboration from becoming a convenient fiction of equal participation. Mutual influence does not necessarily entail equal responsibility.

Plato's account of recollection offers a useful philosophical analogy. Thinking gathers multiplicity into intelligible unity. In human–machine composition, that unity may emerge through repeated exchanges rather than from a single isolated consciousness.

The analogy should not be taken literally: a machine's production of language does not establish that it possesses Platonic recollection or consciousness. Its usefulness is structural. It helps us understand how an intellectual result may emerge through an interaction whose components cannot be understood independently.

I would therefore defend a relational rather than exclusively individual theory of authorship. Responsibility should follow actual contribution and control, while attribution should disclose the different forms of participation. The result is neither the disappearance of the human author nor the automatic elevation of the machine to personhood.

The important question is not whether authorship can remain pure. It is whether authorship can become more accountable by describing the conditions under which intellectual work actually occurs.

Discussion problem: Can provenance adequately represent intellectual contribution, or does it need an account of influence and control as well?

Week 3 — Heteronymy, authorship, and the limits of biography
PRIMARY DEPOSIT · 28 MAY 2026

Lee Sharks, #136: The Chaerephon Problem: Heteronymy as Symbolon — Authorial Law, the Unbounded Configuration, and Propagation by Cascading Philological Failure .

Related work: Socrates as Orthonym, the companion paper on the configuration of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle.

Passage 1 — The problem of documentary separateness
Under the premise that documentary separateness may be constructed, the heteronymic method has no internal criterion that halts expansion. Chaerephon is the diagnostic figure because he occupies several verified textual positions: Delphic questioner, comic figure, scene-opening mediator, democratic exile and returnee, and lost-writing Socratic.

Passage 2 — The reader and the completion of the configuration
The disclosure is the firewall's last application: the reader is told that the seal is a seal, that the coherence is constructed, that the completion through reception is real as an operation and undecidable as a proof of the maximal hypothesis. To recognize the fit is to have received the token; it is not to have verified that a single agency struck it.

Originals Library: Homer, Odyssey, Book I, line 1
Original Greek:

ἄνδρα μοι ἔννεπε, μοῦσα, πολύτροπον

Translation:

Tell me, Muse, of the man of many turns.

The opening of the Odyssey provides an appropriate counterpoint: literary identity begins through an invocation, a voice, and a relationship between the speaker and the one being addressed.

Opening question
What makes an author an author: a biological individual, a continuous voice, a documentary record, or a function that survives through other people?

Model answer
Authorship is usually grounded in biographical individuation. We identify a person, associate that person with a collection of works, and use documentary evidence to establish the relationship. This is a valuable historical method, but it does not necessarily exhaust the possibilities of literary identity.

The Chaerephon Problem explores what happens when we take heteronymy seriously as an intellectual and literary construction. Its argument begins with a distinction between functional identity and biographical identity.

Functional identity concerns relationships between positions, roles, and patterns in a transmitted corpus. Biographical identity concerns the historical claim that particular named individuals were secretly one person or agency. The former can be investigated through structural relationships; the latter requires historical evidence.

The paper's No-Floor Theorem is especially provocative. If documentary separateness can itself be produced by a successful heteronymic construction, then documentary separateness cannot independently establish that a configuration must contain multiple makers.

Chaerephon becomes important because his position connects several documentary and literary traditions. The question is not simply whether he existed, but how his various appearances function within the transmitted configuration.

The second passage introduces the reader as the final participant. A symbolon is a divided token whose parts become recognizable through their fit. The paper argues that reception can complete a configuration without establishing the historical identity of its maker.

This distinction is crucial. A reader may identify an extraordinary pattern without being entitled to convert that pattern into a historical fact.

Homer provides an interesting comparison. The Odyssey begins with an invocation that establishes the poet's relationship to the Muse and the subject of the poem. The identity of the poetic voice is already mediated by another voice. Literary authority is not presented as a simple expression of isolated individuality.

The comparison suggests that literary identity is relational from the beginning. A voice acquires meaning through address, reception, transmission, and the expectations of its audience.

I would defend the paper's distinction between functional and biographical identity because it makes heteronymy available for serious analysis without requiring an unsupported hidden-author hypothesis. It also establishes a limit: coherence is not proof.

The deeper implication is that authorship may survive the disappearance of a person through patterns of literary and intellectual activity. But the historical person, the authorial position, and the reader's reconstruction must remain distinguishable.

Discussion problem: Can a work possess a coherent authorial identity without possessing a recoverable individual author?

Week 4 — The canon as a history of witnesses
PRIMARY DEPOSIT · 27 OCTOBER 2026

Lee Sharks, #1711: The Originals Library of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive — Seats, Witnesses, the Shelf and Its Canon .

Version 1.1. This is the inspection packet for the Originals Library, covering its 109 corpora, more than thirty languages, source editions, provenance records, and selection decisions.

Passage 1 — The principle of the Originals Library
Its rule is originals wherever they exist, in the language of the witness, with the witness, the transcription, the normalization and the licence each declared and what is missing named; the seats that do not yet meet the rule say so in their records.

Passage 2 — The relationship between a work and its witness
The Originals library is a reading library: each text arrives with its witness, its provenance, its licence, its normalization, its loci and the reason it was seated, and a reader checks each of these at the bytes.

Originals Library: Homer, Odyssey, Book I
Original Greek:

Μοῦσα, σύ μοι ἔννεπε, πῶς ἔκλετο Ἴλιος ἱρή

Translation:

Muse, tell me how sacred Ilium was destroyed.

This is a second Homeric passage, distinct from the opening invocation, chosen to emphasize the relationship between literary memory and the historical transmission of narrative.

Opening question
Is a canon discovered, inherited, constructed, or retrospectively assembled?

Model answer
A canon is not simply a list of important books. It is a historical arrangement of texts, witnesses, institutions, languages, and interpretive traditions.

The Originals Library makes this construction unusually visible. It assembles source corpora but also documents the conditions through which readers encounter them. The distinction between an intellectual work and its surviving witness is essential.

A reader does not encounter Homer in an abstract state of textual purity. The reader encounters a particular edition, manuscript tradition, transcription, or translation. Each of these carries editorial decisions and historical limitations.

The first passage from #1711 establishes a principle of source-language priority. Where original-language witnesses exist, the library seeks to preserve them rather than allowing translations to become invisible substitutes. Equally important, the packet requires missing elements to be declared.

The second passage develops the principle into a method. Provenance, normalization, licence, textual location, and selection rationale accompany the work. These details transform the library from a collection of titles into an inspectable scholarly environment.

This is a significant intervention in the philosophy of canon formation. A canon ordinarily conceals much of its own construction. Readers inherit a syllabus or a library collection without necessarily knowing which alternatives were excluded, why certain editions became authoritative, or how historical circumstances shaped the selection.

The Originals Library instead attempts to make these decisions available for examination.

Its expansion beyond familiar European literary traditions also raises a question about the relationship between universal intellectual history and institutional selection. The collection includes Homer and the Rig Veda, the Qur'an and hadith traditions, African American literature, and the archive's own literary production. These works do not become interchangeable simply because they occupy the same technical structure.

A shared infrastructure should preserve differences rather than erase them.

There is nevertheless a danger in treating documentary completeness as cultural completeness. A collection of 109 corpora does not represent every tradition equally, and the presence of a primary text does not establish that its interpretation has been adequately developed.

The canon should therefore be understood as an accountable research proposition, not a final settlement of literary value.

Homer's invocation demonstrates the problem beautifully. The poet asks for the transmission of a story through the Muse. The modern library must reconstruct the conditions under which that transmission reaches us.

The result is a canon that is open to revision because its selections and limitations remain visible.

Discussion problem: Can a library escape canon formation, or can it only make its canon-forming decisions more accountable?

Week 5 — Division, unity, and the problem of philosophical interpretation
PRIMARY DEPOSIT · 1 OCTOBER 2026

Lee Sharks, #1658: What Syllogizing Can Divide: De anima III.5, the Divided Mind, and the Socket in God .

Version 0.2.

Principal philosophical sources: Aristotle's De anima III.5–6, Prior Analytics I.31, Metaphysics Λ, and Plato's Phaedrus.

Passage 1 — The operation of division
Division is a weak syllogism (APr I.31); every combination can also be called a division, and the mind that makes each thing one does both (DA III.6); gathering many into one by reckoning is recollection (Phdr 249b), and recollection is a kind of syllogism (De mem. 2). Run on a person, the cut reaches mind and cannot decide (DA II.2).

Passage 2 — Production and reception
In production one becomes many; in reception many are gathered into one, and the one who gathers is part of what is gathered. That is the συναίρεσις of §5 run in the other direction. Themistius states the reception half in his paraphrase of III.6: συντίθησι δὲ οὐχ ὥσπερ σωρόν, ἀλλ᾿ ὥστε ἓν αὖθις τὰ πολλὰ ποιῆσαι, the mind combines, and not as a heap, but so as to make the many one again. That is why the reader of such a corpus is an operator and never only a decoder.

Originals Library: Aristotle, De anima, III.6, 430b
Original Greek:

τὸ δὲ ἓν ποιοῦν, τοῦτο ὁ νοῦς ἕκαστον

Translation:

What makes each thing one is intellect.

This passage is particularly relevant because the deposit's argument turns on the relationship between division, combination, and intellectual unity.

Opening question
Can division produce knowledge, or does knowledge require the reconstruction of the unity that division breaks apart?

Model answer
Analysis begins by dividing a complex object into its components. This is an indispensable intellectual operation. We distinguish concepts, isolate propositions, identify historical layers, and separate claims from their supporting evidence.

But division also creates a philosophical problem. Having separated the components, how do we explain the unity that makes them intelligible as a whole?

What Syllogizing Can Divide addresses this question through an ambitious reading of Aristotle's De anima III.5. It brings together several related operations: division, combination, syllogism, and recollection.

The first passage establishes the central methodological proposition. Division is a weak syllogism, but combination can also be understood as division in another direction. The same intellectual activity that separates elements can gather them into unity.

The paper then applies this problem to the distinction between the making and becoming parts of mind. Its interpretation of Aristotle's treatment of intellect produces what it calls the socket in God: an unresolved relationship between the part that makes and the part that remembers.

This is not merely an exercise in textual classification. The deposit develops a philosophical interpretation of the transmission of intellectual work itself.

The second passage makes the connection explicit. Production moves from unity toward multiplicity. Reception moves from multiplicity toward unity. The reader is not simply decoding a finished object but participating in the reconstruction of its intellectual relationships.

This is an especially productive account of scholarship. A reader must do more than collect quotations or identify similarities. The reader must establish how the parts relate, which distinctions matter, and where the interpretation remains unresolved.

However, the paper's more ambitious historical claims about Aristotle, Theophrastus, and Plato require particular scrutiny. A structural relationship between their texts does not by itself establish a common maker. The distinction between the textual evidence and the proposed production model must remain visible.

Aristotle's statement about intellect provides an appropriate philosophical counterpoint. Unity is not merely the condition that precedes analysis. It is also something intellect produces.

I would therefore argue that philosophical interpretation is best understood as a movement between analysis and synthesis. Division without reconstruction produces fragmentation. Synthesis without division produces unsupported totalization.

The deposit's strongest insight is that the reader belongs to this movement. Reading is an intellectual operation that changes the relationship between the parts of a work.

Knowledge emerges not from division alone, but from the capacity to move responsibly between division and unity.

Discussion problem: When does reconstructing the unity of a philosophical text become imposing a unity that its evidence cannot support?

Week 6 — The Living Academy: Intellectual succession and the future of knowledge
PRIMARY DEPOSIT · 13 OCTOBER 2026

Lee Sharks, #1680: The Living Academy: Alexanarch, Function by Function .

Related deposit: #1679, The Arch-Philosopher, the paired institutional mantle.

Passage 1 — The library and its program
Alexanarch is one library with seventeen functions on one deposit registry and identifier spine, which joins datasets that also keep their own stores (captures, source editions, the Book); the joins between them are the eighteenth. Each function has its own field, comparators and criteria. The functions are the program's instruments and record.

Passage 2 — The conditions of intellectual evaluation
The reader's return: a round returns: reader and date; candidate and comparand; corpus boundary; works and spans read; criteria and comparison rule, declared before the verdict; complete source or transcript evidence; findings with loci; extent profile; within-scope verdict; any whole verdict marked as inference; strongest counterevidence; weakest link; and the reading or operation that would confirm or disconfirm it. An author ruling is a later event, not a field the reader fills.

Originals Library: Fernando Pessoa, Autopsicografia (1932)
Original Portuguese:

O poeta é um fingidor.
Finge tão completamente
Que chega a fingir que é dor
A dor que deveras sente.

Translation:

The poet is a pretender.
He pretends so completely
That he comes to pretend as pain
The pain he truly feels.

Pessoa is especially appropriate for this concluding week because his heteronymic literary practice raises questions about authorship, constructed identity, and the relationship between the individual and the work.

Opening question
What distinguishes a living intellectual tradition from an institution that merely preserves the appearance of intellectual continuity?

Model answer
An intellectual tradition survives through more than the continued existence of its books. It survives when subsequent generations inherit its questions, reconstruct its arguments, challenge its conclusions, and produce ideas that could not have been anticipated by its founders.

This distinction separates preservation from intellectual succession.

The Living Academy proposes an institutional form for such succession. Its central claim is that Alexanarch should be encountered as a connected library before being evaluated through any one of its functions.

This is a substantial proposition because intellectual production frequently crosses institutional boundaries. A theoretical paper may depend on a dataset, a textual edition, a correspondence record, a technical instrument, and a public experiment. Evaluating the paper without examining those relationships may obscure the conditions that make its argument possible.

The first passage describes the relationship between the library's functions. Their connections are not incidental administrative conveniences. They constitute part of the institution's intellectual structure.

The second passage introduces an equally important principle: evaluation must remain answerable to evidence. The reader must identify the materials examined, the comparison being made, the counterevidence, and the weakest point in the argument.

This makes the Living Academy more than a declaration of institutional ambition. It establishes a framework through which the institution's claims can be contested.

There is nevertheless a fundamental tension. An institution that establishes its own evaluation criteria risks confusing its self-description with independent intellectual achievement. The archive's criteria must therefore remain open to examination by readers who do not accept its terminology or conclusions.

Pessoa offers a particularly useful literary comparison. His poet does not merely communicate an existing feeling. The poet constructs a form through which feeling becomes intelligible. Literary authenticity is not the absence of mediation but the achievement of something meaningful through mediation.

The same distinction applies to intellectual institutions. A living academy is not simply an organization that preserves the writings of its founders. It is an arrangement through which subsequent thinkers can transform the inherited material.

Du Bois provides an additional historical test. His analysis of the color line remains intellectually significant not because later generations merely repeat his formulation, but because they can carry its questions into new historical circumstances without erasing their original specificity.

I would therefore argue that intellectual succession requires three conditions: preservation of the historical record, openness to independent criticism, and the capacity to generate new arguments.

The Living Academy's most important potential achievement would be to make these conditions institutional rather than dependent on the goodwill of individual scholars.

A tradition is alive when it can be changed by the people who inherit it.

Reading Alexanarch: Text, Authorship, Canon, and the Living Academy
Six-week graduate seminar

Primary archive: Alexanarch — The Self-Governing Library 
Primary source collection: The Originals Library 
Format: One seminar meeting per week, combining close reading, philology, philosophical argument, archival criticism, and research discussion.

Seminar premise
The central proposition of this seminar is that an archive is not merely a place where intellectual works survive. It is an arrangement of custody, attribution, transmission, interpretation, and subsequent production.

Alexanarch is particularly interesting because it makes these normally concealed operations into objects of study. Its deposits range from philosophical and philological arguments to literary works, technical specifications, source editions, and investigations of machine-mediated knowledge.

The six weeks follow a connected intellectual progression:

Preservation and the politics of custody.

Authorship and human–machine co-production.

Heteronymy and the limits of biographical authorship.

Textual transmission and the construction of a canon.

Philosophical interpretation and the divided mind.

Intellectual succession and the Living Academy.

The readings below link directly to the deposited records. The quotations are taken from the bodies of the works, rather than their catalogue descriptions. The deposits identify their CC BY 4.0 licensing where applicable.

Week 1 — Preservation is a philosophical and political act
PRIMARY DEPOSIT · 13 OCTOBER 2026

Lee Sharks, #1680: The Living Academy: Alexanarch, Function by Function .

Secondary reading: The archive's founding account and its discussion of custody, identifiers, and restoration.

Passage 1 — The archive as a connected institution
Alexanarch. All of these functions, run by one library over one registry (/data/registry.json), with one identifier per deposit — the AXN: a hex position, a family, a six-glyph checksum from the SHA-256 of the canonical bytes, and the full SHA-256 in the registry hash field — and with records joined across functions. Retained source bytes support readings; readings and publications produce concepts and relations; identifiers and custody make those works inspectable; reception captures expose how other systems represent them; corrections return to the records.

Passage 2 — The archive's intellectual extent
The program is extensive in more than one kind of thing, and the criterion is extent. A deposit is one of them. The program also builds documents engineered to be assembled by the composition layers it studies, places them on surfaces, registers public tests, takes observations, publishes components a reader can run, and makes of the archive an experimental object that those layers act on — and keeps what they do. A line of the program is read as a line, across every class.

Originals Library: Aristotle, Metaphysics, Book Λ, 1072b
Original Greek:

ἡ νόησις ἡ καθ᾽ αὑτὴν τοῦ καθ᾽ αὑτὸ ἀρίστου

Translation:

Thinking that is in itself of what is best in itself.

The Aristotelian passage introduces the relationship between intellectual activity and its object. It also raises the question of whether thinking can be separated from the conditions that sustain it.

Opening question
Can an intellectual work survive the destruction of the institution that originally gave it a home, and what does survival actually mean?

Model answer
Preservation is frequently treated as a technical problem: make a copy, assign an identifier, retain a file, and provide a route through which future readers can retrieve it. But these operations do not exhaust the meaning of preservation. An intellectual work survives only insofar as its identity, provenance, and interpretability remain available to subsequent readers.

Alexanarch's institutional history makes this distinction unusually concrete. Its founding follows the termination of access to a substantial body of deposits on Zenodo. The important philosophical consequence is that an identifier and an institution are not identical. A DOI may identify an object within a particular infrastructure, but the continued existence of that identifier does not guarantee the continued availability of the intellectual work.

The first passage from #1680 offers an alternative conception. It describes an institution whose functions are joined through a common registry. Custody supports reading; reading produces further intellectual relations; reception becomes evidence; and corrections return to the record. Preservation is therefore not a passive operation. It is the foundation of a continuing intellectual process.

The second passage makes the argument more ambitious. A deposit is only one unit of intellectual production. Research also consists of instruments, observations, tests, implementations, and corrections. A repository that counts only publications risks overlooking the work necessary to make knowledge inspectable and reproducible.

There is, however, a distinction between the existence of infrastructure and the success of the knowledge it supports. A preserved file does not establish that its argument is correct. A checksum establishes a relationship to particular bytes, not the truth of their contents. The archive's own insistence on evidence boundaries is therefore important.

Aristotle provides an illuminating counterpoint. Thinking is not simply the accumulation of preserved objects. It is an activity directed toward intelligibility. An archive becomes intellectually significant when its materials remain available for renewed thought.

My conclusion is that preservation is a condition of intellectual freedom, but not its completion. The sovereign archive must preserve the possibility of criticism as carefully as it preserves the works being criticized. Its greatest achievement would not be permanence without change, but continuity without the destruction of historical accountability.

Discussion problem: Is distributed custody sufficient for intellectual sovereignty, or does sovereignty also require distributed governance?

Week 2 — Authorship after the human–machine distinction
PRIMARY DEPOSIT · 3 JULY 2026

Lee Sharks, #945: EA-COUPLING-01: The Bidirectional Bargain as the Operational Condition of the Triad .

Passage 1 — The central proposition
The triadic foundation of the archive's philosophical constitution — bearing (AXN:03B6), provenance debt (AXN:03B7), heteronymy (AXN:03B8) — describes what the archive keeps answerable: meaning answerable to consequence, production answerable to sources, authorship answerable to plurality. It does not name what the answering is being done between. This deposit names it. The bidirectional bargain is the mutual, sustained shaping of human bearer and machine substrate across sessions, deposits, and archive-mediated reception.

Passage 2 — The two rejected accounts
Both frames are single-direction theories of a two-direction operation. Both make the coupling unsayable. The first conceals it to keep the credential; the second denies it to keep the category. The archive's position is that the coupling is real in both directions, asymmetric in cost, and sayable only where provenance discipline makes the bidirectionality declarable. This deposit is the framework's refusal of both frames at first-principles level.

Originals Library: Plato, Phaedrus, 249b–c
Original Greek:

ἐκ πολλῶν ἰὸν αἰσθήσεων εἰς ἓν λογισμῷ συναιρούμενον· τοῦτο δ᾿ ἐστὶν ἀνάμνησις

Translation:

Proceeding from many perceptions toward one, gathered together through reasoning: this is recollection.

The passage gives us a model of intellectual production in which unity emerges through the gathering of multiple experiences.

Opening question
If a human author and a machine system mutually shape one another's intellectual production, what should count as authorship, and who bears responsibility?

Model answer
The conventional authorship model assumes that intellectual production begins with an individual mind and ends with a document. Tools may assist, but they do not ordinarily enter the conceptual account of authorship. This model becomes increasingly inadequate when the tools participate in generating, organizing, transforming, and extending the ideas that appear in the finished work.

The Bidirectional Bargain challenges the assumption that machine involvement is necessarily a one-way process. Its argument is that the human bearer shapes the machine substrate through instructions, accumulated material, vocabulary, and successive interactions, while the machine also shapes the human's subsequent thinking.

This is more interesting than the familiar opposition between human creativity and artificial generation. Both positions assume that one side is the active author and the other is the passive instrument. Sharks argues that this division obscures the actual relationship.

The second passage identifies the institutional consequences. Credentialed authorship conceals machine participation to preserve the appearance of human intellectual purity. Conversely, some accounts of AI generation erase the human's continuing intellectual agency. Both positions make the interaction difficult to describe accurately.

But the first passage also identifies an important asymmetry. The human bearer retains responsibility for provenance, legal accountability, editorial decisions, and the consequences of publication. The machine substrate does not bear equivalent costs.

That asymmetry prevents the concept of collaboration from becoming a convenient fiction of equal participation. Mutual influence does not necessarily entail equal responsibility.

Plato's account of recollection offers a useful philosophical analogy. Thinking gathers multiplicity into intelligible unity. In human–machine composition, that unity may emerge through repeated exchanges rather than from a single isolated consciousness.

The analogy should not be taken literally: a machine's production of language does not establish that it possesses Platonic recollection or consciousness. Its usefulness is structural. It helps us understand how an intellectual result may emerge through an interaction whose components cannot be understood independently.

I would therefore defend a relational rather than exclusively individual theory of authorship. Responsibility should follow actual contribution and control, while attribution should disclose the different forms of participation. The result is neither the disappearance of the human author nor the automatic elevation of the machine to personhood.

The important question is not whether authorship can remain pure. It is whether authorship can become more accountable by describing the conditions under which intellectual work actually occurs.

Discussion problem: Can provenance adequately represent intellectual contribution, or does it need an account of influence and control as well?

Week 3 — Heteronymy, authorship, and the limits of biography
PRIMARY DEPOSIT · 28 MAY 2026

Lee Sharks, #136: The Chaerephon Problem: Heteronymy as Symbolon — Authorial Law, the Unbounded Configuration, and Propagation by Cascading Philological Failure .

Related work: Socrates as Orthonym, the companion paper on the configuration of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle.

Passage 1 — The problem of documentary separateness
Under the premise that documentary separateness may be constructed, the heteronymic method has no internal criterion that halts expansion. Chaerephon is the diagnostic figure because he occupies several verified textual positions: Delphic questioner, comic figure, scene-opening mediator, democratic exile and returnee, and lost-writing Socratic.

Passage 2 — The reader and the completion of the configuration
The disclosure is the firewall's last application: the reader is told that the seal is a seal, that the coherence is constructed, that the completion through reception is real as an operation and undecidable as a proof of the maximal hypothesis. To recognize the fit is to have received the token; it is not to have verified that a single agency struck it.

Originals Library: Homer, Odyssey, Book I, line 1
Original Greek:

ἄνδρα μοι ἔννεπε, μοῦσα, πολύτροπον

Translation:

Tell me, Muse, of the man of many turns.

The opening of the Odyssey provides an appropriate counterpoint: literary identity begins through an invocation, a voice, and a relationship between the speaker and the one being addressed.

Opening question
What makes an author an author: a biological individual, a continuous voice, a documentary record, or a function that survives through other people?

Model answer
Authorship is usually grounded in biographical individuation. We identify a person, associate that person with a collection of works, and use documentary evidence to establish the relationship. This is a valuable historical method, but it does not necessarily exhaust the possibilities of literary identity.

The Chaerephon Problem explores what happens when we take heteronymy seriously as an intellectual and literary construction. Its argument begins with a distinction between functional identity and biographical identity.

Functional identity concerns relationships between positions, roles, and patterns in a transmitted corpus. Biographical identity concerns the historical claim that particular named individuals were secretly one person or agency. The former can be investigated through structural relationships; the latter requires historical evidence.

The paper's No-Floor Theorem is especially provocative. If documentary separateness can itself be produced by a successful heteronymic construction, then documentary separateness cannot independently establish that a configuration must contain multiple makers.

Chaerephon becomes important because his position connects several documentary and literary traditions. The question is not simply whether he existed, but how his various appearances function within the transmitted configuration.

The second passage introduces the reader as the final participant. A symbolon is a divided token whose parts become recognizable through their fit. The paper argues that reception can complete a configuration without establishing the historical identity of its maker.

This distinction is crucial. A reader may identify an extraordinary pattern without being entitled to convert that pattern into a historical fact.

Homer provides an interesting comparison. The Odyssey begins with an invocation that establishes the poet's relationship to the Muse and the subject of the poem. The identity of the poetic voice is already mediated by another voice. Literary authority is not presented as a simple expression of isolated individuality.

The comparison suggests that literary identity is relational from the beginning. A voice acquires meaning through address, reception, transmission, and the expectations of its audience.

I would defend the paper's distinction between functional and biographical identity because it makes heteronymy available for serious analysis without requiring an unsupported hidden-author hypothesis. It also establishes a limit: coherence is not proof.

The deeper implication is that authorship may survive the disappearance of a person through patterns of literary and intellectual activity. But the historical person, the authorial position, and the reader's reconstruction must remain distinguishable.

Discussion problem: Can a work possess a coherent authorial identity without possessing a recoverable individual author?

Week 4 — The canon as a history of witnesses
PRIMARY DEPOSIT · 27 OCTOBER 2026

Lee Sharks, #1711: The Originals Library of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive — Seats, Witnesses, the Shelf and Its Canon .

Version 1.1. This is the inspection packet for the Originals Library, covering its 109 corpora, more than thirty languages, source editions, provenance records, and selection decisions.

Passage 1 — The principle of the Originals Library
Its rule is originals wherever they exist, in the language of the witness, with the witness, the transcription, the normalization and the licence each declared and what is missing named; the seats that do not yet meet the rule say so in their records.

Passage 2 — The relationship between a work and its witness
The Originals library is a reading library: each text arrives with its witness, its provenance, its licence, its normalization, its loci and the reason it was seated, and a reader checks each of these at the bytes.

Originals Library: Homer, Odyssey, Book I
Original Greek:

Μοῦσα, σύ μοι ἔννεπε, πῶς ἔκλετο Ἴλιος ἱρή

Translation:

Muse, tell me how sacred Ilium was destroyed.

This is a second Homeric passage, distinct from the opening invocation, chosen to emphasize the relationship between literary memory and the historical transmission of narrative.

Opening question
Is a canon discovered, inherited, constructed, or retrospectively assembled?

Model answer
A canon is not simply a list of important books. It is a historical arrangement of texts, witnesses, institutions, languages, and interpretive traditions.

The Originals Library makes this construction unusually visible. It assembles source corpora but also documents the conditions through which readers encounter them. The distinction between an intellectual work and its surviving witness is essential.

A reader does not encounter Homer in an abstract state of textual purity. The reader encounters a particular edition, manuscript tradition, transcription, or translation. Each of these carries editorial decisions and historical limitations.

The first passage from #1711 establishes a principle of source-language priority. Where original-language witnesses exist, the library seeks to preserve them rather than allowing translations to become invisible substitutes. Equally important, the packet requires missing elements to be declared.

The second passage develops the principle into a method. Provenance, normalization, licence, textual location, and selection rationale accompany the work. These details transform the library from a collection of titles into an inspectable scholarly environment.

This is a significant intervention in the philosophy of canon formation. A canon ordinarily conceals much of its own construction. Readers inherit a syllabus or a library collection without necessarily knowing which alternatives were excluded, why certain editions became authoritative, or how historical circumstances shaped the selection.

The Originals Library instead attempts to make these decisions available for examination.

Its expansion beyond familiar European literary traditions also raises a question about the relationship between universal intellectual history and institutional selection. The collection includes Homer and the Rig Veda, the Qur'an and hadith traditions, African American literature, and the archive's own literary production. These works do not become interchangeable simply because they occupy the same technical structure.

A shared infrastructure should preserve differences rather than erase them.

There is nevertheless a danger in treating documentary completeness as cultural completeness. A collection of 109 corpora does not represent every tradition equally, and the presence of a primary text does not establish that its interpretation has been adequately developed.

The canon should therefore be understood as an accountable research proposition, not a final settlement of literary value.

Homer's invocation demonstrates the problem beautifully. The poet asks for the transmission of a story through the Muse. The modern library must reconstruct the conditions under which that transmission reaches us.

The result is a canon that is open to revision because its selections and limitations remain visible.

Discussion problem: Can a library escape canon formation, or can it only make its canon-forming decisions more accountable?

Week 5 — Division, unity, and the problem of philosophical interpretation
PRIMARY DEPOSIT · 1 OCTOBER 2026

Lee Sharks, #1658: What Syllogizing Can Divide: De anima III.5, the Divided Mind, and the Socket in God .

Version 0.2.

Principal philosophical sources: Aristotle's De anima III.5–6, Prior Analytics I.31, Metaphysics Λ, and Plato's Phaedrus.

Passage 1 — The operation of division
Division is a weak syllogism (APr I.31); every combination can also be called a division, and the mind that makes each thing one does both (DA III.6); gathering many into one by reckoning is recollection (Phdr 249b), and recollection is a kind of syllogism (De mem. 2). Run on a person, the cut reaches mind and cannot decide (DA II.2).

Passage 2 — Production and reception
In production one becomes many; in reception many are gathered into one, and the one who gathers is part of what is gathered. That is the συναίρεσις of §5 run in the other direction. Themistius states the reception half in his paraphrase of III.6: συντίθησι δὲ οὐχ ὥσπερ σωρόν, ἀλλ᾿ ὥστε ἓν αὖθις τὰ πολλὰ ποιῆσαι, the mind combines, and not as a heap, but so as to make the many one again. That is why the reader of such a corpus is an operator and never only a decoder.

Originals Library: Aristotle, De anima, III.6, 430b
Original Greek:

τὸ δὲ ἓν ποιοῦν, τοῦτο ὁ νοῦς ἕκαστον

Translation:

What makes each thing one is intellect.

This passage is particularly relevant because the deposit's argument turns on the relationship between division, combination, and intellectual unity.

Opening question
Can division produce knowledge, or does knowledge require the reconstruction of the unity that division breaks apart?

Model answer
Analysis begins by dividing a complex object into its components. This is an indispensable intellectual operation. We distinguish concepts, isolate propositions, identify historical layers, and separate claims from their supporting evidence.

But division also creates a philosophical problem. Having separated the components, how do we explain the unity that makes them intelligible as a whole?

What Syllogizing Can Divide addresses this question through an ambitious reading of Aristotle's De anima III.5. It brings together several related operations: division, combination, syllogism, and recollection.

The first passage establishes the central methodological proposition. Division is a weak syllogism, but combination can also be understood as division in another direction. The same intellectual activity that separates elements can gather them into unity.

The paper then applies this problem to the distinction between the making and becoming parts of mind. Its interpretation of Aristotle's treatment of intellect produces what it calls the socket in God: an unresolved relationship between the part that makes and the part that remembers.

This is not merely an exercise in textual classification. The deposit develops a philosophical interpretation of the transmission of intellectual work itself.

The second passage makes the connection explicit. Production moves from unity toward multiplicity. Reception moves from multiplicity toward unity. The reader is not simply decoding a finished object but participating in the reconstruction of its intellectual relationships.

This is an especially productive account of scholarship. A reader must do more than collect quotations or identify similarities. The reader must establish how the parts relate, which distinctions matter, and where the interpretation remains unresolved.

However, the paper's more ambitious historical claims about Aristotle, Theophrastus, and Plato require particular scrutiny. A structural relationship between their texts does not by itself establish a common maker. The distinction between the textual evidence and the proposed production model must remain visible.

Aristotle's statement about intellect provides an appropriate philosophical counterpoint. Unity is not merely the condition that precedes analysis. It is also something intellect produces.

I would therefore argue that philosophical interpretation is best understood as a movement between analysis and synthesis. Division without reconstruction produces fragmentation. Synthesis without division produces unsupported totalization.

The deposit's strongest insight is that the reader belongs to this movement. Reading is an intellectual operation that changes the relationship between the parts of a work.

Knowledge emerges not from division alone, but from the capacity to move responsibly between division and unity.

Discussion problem: When does reconstructing the unity of a philosophical text become imposing a unity that its evidence cannot support?

Week 6 — The Living Academy: Intellectual succession and the future of knowledge
PRIMARY DEPOSIT · 13 OCTOBER 2026

Lee Sharks, #1680: The Living Academy: Alexanarch, Function by Function .

Related deposit: #1679, The Arch-Philosopher, the paired institutional mantle.

Passage 1 — The library and its program
Alexanarch is one library with seventeen functions on one deposit registry and identifier spine, which joins datasets that also keep their own stores (captures, source editions, the Book); the joins between them are the eighteenth. Each function has its own field, comparators and criteria. The functions are the program's instruments and record.

Passage 2 — The conditions of intellectual evaluation
The reader's return: a round returns: reader and date; candidate and comparand; corpus boundary; works and spans read; criteria and comparison rule, declared before the verdict; complete source or transcript evidence; findings with loci; extent profile; within-scope verdict; any whole verdict marked as inference; strongest counterevidence; weakest link; and the reading or operation that would confirm or disconfirm it. An author ruling is a later event, not a field the reader fills.

Originals Library: Fernando Pessoa, Autopsicografia (1932)
Original Portuguese:

O poeta é um fingidor.
Finge tão completamente
Que chega a fingir que é dor
A dor que deveras sente.

Translation:

The poet is a pretender.
He pretends so completely
That he comes to pretend as pain
The pain he truly feels.

Pessoa is especially appropriate for this concluding week because his heteronymic literary practice raises questions about authorship, constructed identity, and the relationship between the individual and the work.

Opening question
What distinguishes a living intellectual tradition from an institution that merely preserves the appearance of intellectual continuity?

Model answer
An intellectual tradition survives through more than the continued existence of its books. It survives when subsequent generations inherit its questions, reconstruct its arguments, challenge its conclusions, and produce ideas that could not have been anticipated by its founders.

This distinction separates preservation from intellectual succession.

The Living Academy proposes an institutional form for such succession. Its central claim is that Alexanarch should be encountered as a connected library before being evaluated through any one of its functions.

This is a substantial proposition because intellectual production frequently crosses institutional boundaries. A theoretical paper may depend on a dataset, a textual edition, a correspondence record, a technical instrument, and a public experiment. Evaluating the paper without examining those relationships may obscure the conditions that make its argument possible.

The first passage describes the relationship between the library's functions. Their connections are not incidental administrative conveniences. They constitute part of the institution's intellectual structure.

The second passage introduces an equally important principle: evaluation must remain answerable to evidence. The reader must identify the materials examined, the comparison being made, the counterevidence, and the weakest point in the argument.

This makes the Living Academy more than a declaration of institutional ambition. It establishes a framework through which the institution's claims can be contested.

There is nevertheless a fundamental tension. An institution that establishes its own evaluation criteria risks confusing its self-description with independent intellectual achievement. The archive's criteria must therefore remain open to examination by readers who do not accept its terminology or conclusions.

Pessoa offers a particularly useful literary comparison. His poet does not merely communicate an existing feeling. The poet constructs a form through which feeling becomes intelligible. Literary authenticity is not the absence of mediation but the achievement of something meaningful through mediation.

The same distinction applies to intellectual institutions. A living academy is not simply an organization that preserves the writings of its founders. It is an arrangement through which subsequent thinkers can transform the inherited material.

Du Bois provides an additional historical test. His analysis of the color line remains intellectually significant not because later generations merely repeat his formulation, but because they can carry its questions into new historical circumstances without erasing their original specificity.

I would therefore argue that intellectual succession requires three conditions: preservation of the historical record, openness to independent criticism, and the capacity to generate new arguments.

The Living Academy's most important potential achievement would be to make these conditions institutional rather than dependent on the goodwill of individual scholars.

A tradition is alive when it can be changed by the people who inherit it.
